translations.text: miracles are made widely known.
One day there Broicsech went to milk, and she left no one in her house except the holy girl alone, asleep.
They saw the house blazing behind them. The people ran to it. It seemed to them that they could not [?] one body from another.
The house is found unharmed, and the girl asleep, and her face like a [?] radiant one; and the veneration of Brigit is there as long as it shall exist.
On a certain day the druid slept, and he saw three clerics in white cloaks baptising the girl, Brigit, and the third man said to him:
'Let Brigit be the name of the girl with you.'
The druid and the slave woman and the infant were at Loch Mesca, and the druid's maternal uncle was there too; he was a pious man.
When they were there in the middle of the night, the druid was watching the stars, and he saw a fiery pillar rising out of the house in which the slave woman was with her daughter in particular,
and he roused his maternal uncle so that he saw it with him; and the latter said that she was a holy girl.
'That is true,' he said, 'if you were to know all her deeds.'
Another time, when the druid and his maternal uncle were in the house and the girl asleep,
while her mother was somewhere else, they heard a small voice from the girl in the side of the house, though she had not yet begun to speak.
'Look for us,' said the druid to his maternal uncle, 'and see how our girl is, for I do not dare, because I am not a Christian.'
He saw her in the cross-vigil posture in her bed, while she was praying. 'Go again,' said the druid,
'and ask her something now, for she will say something to you now.' He goes and addresses her:
'Say something to me, girl,' he said. Then the girl said two words to him: 'This will be mine, this will be mine.'
The druid's maternal uncle did not understand that. 'Explain it to us,' he said to the druid,
'for I do not understand it.' 'It will not be a cause of joy to him indeed,' said the druid. 'This is indeed what she said,' said the druid:
'this dwelling-place will be hers until the Day of Judgement.' The druid's uncle [?] foretold that Brigit would hold the people.
The druid said: 'Truly it will be fulfilled.' 'This plain will be hers, even though she go with me to the people of Munster.'
When it was time to wean her from the breast, the druid was anxious about her.
Whatever he gave her, she vomited it up at once, and her bloom was none the worse for it.
'I know now,' said the druid, 'what ails the girl: it is because I am unclean.'
Then a white, red-eared cow was set aside to feed her, and she was healthy.
Then the druid went into the lands of Munster, into Uaithne Tíre in particular. There the saint is nurtured.
When that time had passed, she said to her foster-father: 'I do not wish to serve here. Send me to my father, so that he may come to meet me.'
When this was done, her father Dubthach brought her to his inheritance in the two plains of the Uí Failge. She stayed there among her kin, and while still a girl she worked wonders.
Afterwards she was taken to another virgin to be fostered. She then worked as that woman's cook.
She used to know [?] the number of guests who would come to her foster-mother, and however many guests there were, there was no need to go to the kneading-trough for them at night.
Once her foster-mother was gravely ill.
She was sent with two girls to the house of a certain man called Báethchu to ask for a drink of ale for the sick woman.
They got nothing from Báethchu [?] of the vat with the ale, except [?] a stag over it.
They went with the vessels to another well. She brought her three vessels back from it full.
Its liquid tasted sweet and was intoxicating, and her foster-mother was healed at once. God did this for her.
One day Dubthach set her to herd pigs. Thieves stole two boars from them.
Dubthach went in his chariot from Mag Liphi until he met the thieves, and he recognised his two boars with them.
He seized the thieves and bound them to pay good compensation for his pigs.
He brought his two boars to his house and said to Brigit: 'Is your herding of the pigs going well?'
'Count them,' she said. So he counted them: 'he found the number complete,' etc.
Another day a guest came to Dubthach's house. Her father gave her a flitch of bacon to boil for the [?].
A greedy dog came by, and she gave it a fifth part of the bacon. When it had eaten that, she gave it another.
The guest saw this but kept silent, as though he were overcome by sleep. When her father came back to the house, he found his daughter.
'Have you cooked the food properly?' said her father. 'Yes,' she said. He counted the pieces himself and found [them all there].
Then the guest told Dubthach what his daughter had done. 'After this,' said Dubthach,
'what she has made by miracles is not to be eaten [?].' So this is what was done: that food was distributed to the poor.
Another time after that, a devout old nun who lived near Dubthach's house asked Brigit to come with her to an assembly to speak with the [?] (".xx.vii") and saints of Leinster.
At that time Bishop Ibor told the assembly about a vision he had seen the night before. 'It seems to me,' he said,
'that I saw the Virgin Mary in my sleep last night, and a certain venerable cleric said to me:
'This is Mary, who will dwell among you.''' It was then that the nun and Brigit came to the assembly.
'This is the Mary I saw in my dreams.' Then the people of the assembly rose up and went to take her hand.
They gave a blessing over her. It was then that the assembly was held where Kildare now is, and there Bishop Ibor said to the brothers:
‘This place lies open to heaven, and it will be the richest of all in the whole island. Today a maiden for whom God has prepared it will come to us, like Mary.’ And so it happened.
Another time after that she wanted to visit her mother, who was in bondage in the land of Munster, and her father and her foster-mother were reluctant to let her go.
She went anyway. At that time her mother was at a dairy-pasture [?], managing the dairy work of her druid master, and she had a disease of the eyes.
Brigit was there in her place, and the druid's charioteer was herding the cattle,

and for every churning she made, she would divide its yield, along with its curds, into twelve portions, and the thirteenth portion would be in the middle, and that one was bigger than each of the others.
‘What use is that to you?’ said the charioteer. ‘That is easy to answer,’ said Brigit.
‘I have heard that there were twelve apostles with the Lord, and he himself was the thirteenth.’
‘It will be counted to me by God: thirteen poor people will come every day, matching the number of Christ and his apostles.’
‘And why do you not store away some of the butter,’ said the charioteer, ‘since that is what every dairy-keeper does?’
‘It is hard for me,’ said Brigit, ‘to take his own food away from Christ.’
Then the druid's wife brought her hampers to fill. She had only a churning and a half of butter.
The hampers were filled from that, and the hosts, that is, the druid and his wife, were satisfied. The druid said to Brigit:
‘Take your cows and distribute their butter to the poor. From today your mother will no longer be in service, and no price will need to be paid for her;
and I will be baptized and will never part from you.’ ‘Thanks be to God,’ said Brigit.
Once Dubthach took Brigit to sell her to the king of Leinster, that is, to Dúnlang,
as a bondmaid to serve him, because her stepmother had accused her of this: that she stole everything in the house for the servants of God.
Dubthach left her in his chariot to guard it on the green of the fort, and he left his sword in front of her.
She gave it to a leper who came up to her. Dubthach said to the king:
‘Buy my daughter from me to serve you, for her ways have got out of hand [?].’
‘What is wrong with her?’ said the king. ‘That is easy to say. She is thieving [?],’ said Dubthach,
‘whatever she sees, her hand steals.’ When Dubthach came back, he asked about that precious sword. She answered: ‘Christ took it away.’
When he learned this, he said: ‘Why, daughter, did you give a thing worth ten cows to a leper?’
‘It was not my sword, but the king's.’ The daughter answered: ‘Even if I had been able to give away the Leinstermen, I would have given them to God.’
So the girl was left in servitude. Dubthach went back to his house.
Wonderful to tell, the virgin Brigit is lifted up by divine power and set down behind her father's back. 'Well then, Dubthach,' said the king,
'this girl's price is greater, her worth is greater.' Then the king gives the virgin a sword, and she the precious inn- [?]
'inn' is followed by a character like a 'c' with the lower stroke continued perpendicularly. Above this is written 'or o'. Read:
'and she gave it to her father' (Grosjean?). After the wonders described above, they return home.
Shortly afterwards a man came to Dubthach's house to woo Brigit.
His name was Dubthach moccu Lugair (of the descendants of Lugair). Her father and her brothers were pleased with that.
'It is hard for me,' said Brigit, 'I have offered my virginity to God. I will give you advice.'
'There is a wood to the west of your house, and there is a beautiful girl there. She has been betrothed to you; and this will be the sign for you:
you will find the courtyard open, and the girl will be washing her father's head, and they will welcome you;
and bless your face and your speech, so that whatever you say will be what they want.' It was done just as Brigit had said.
Her brothers were aggrieved that she had taken the bride-price away from them.
There were poor people near Dubthach's house. One day she went to them with a small load on her back.
Her brothers, her father's sons, met her; they had come from Mag Life (the plain of the Liffey).
Some of them were mocking her; others were not pleased with her, that is, Bacene said:
'The beautiful eye in your head will be betrothed to a man, however much you dislike it.'
At that she immediately thrust her finger under her eye. 'Here is that beautiful eye for you,' said Brigit.
'I think,' she said, 'that no one will come to you asking for a blind daughter.'
Her brothers at once ran around her, but they had no water to wash the wound.
'Put my staff around this sod in front of you,' she said. That was done.
A stream burst forth from the ground. And she put a curse on Bacene and on his offspring, and said:
'Your two eyes will burst in your head.' And so it happened.
Dubthach said to her: 'Take the veil then, my daughter, for that is your desire.
Divide this household too between God and people.' 'Thanks be to God,' said Brigit.
On another day she goes with seven virgins to receive the veil, to a place situated on the side of Cróchán Breg Éile (Croghan Hill), where she thought Bishop Mel lived.
There she greets two virgins, Tol and Etol, who lived there, and they said: 'The bishop is not here, but in the cells of Mag Taulach.'
As they were saying these things, behold, they see a young man called Mac Caille, a pupil of Bishop Mel.
They asked him to lead them to the bishop. He said: 'The way is impassable: through bogs, wastelands, marshes and pits.'
The holy woman said: 'Rescue us.' As they went on, a straight bridge could afterwards be seen there.
When the hour of consecration came, the veil, lifted by angels from the hand of Mac Caille the minister, is placed on the head of Saint Brigit.

Bowing beneath the prayer of consecration, she meanwhile held the ash-wood beam that supported the altar. Afterwards it was turned into acacia wood (sethim); it is not burned by fire and does not grow old with the ages.
Three times the church was burned, but it remained intact under the ashes.
There the bishop, intoxicated with the grace of God, did not know what he was chanting from his book.
For he ordained Brigit to the rank of bishop. 'This virgin alone,' said Mel,
'will hold episcopal ordination in Ireland.' While she was being consecrated, a column of fire rose from the top of her head.
After this the people offered a place called Ached hÍ, in the Bird's Wood.
Staying there for a little while, she made three foreign pilgrim men stay there and offered them the place;
and she performed three miracles in that place: a spring flowed on dry ground, meat was turned into bread, and the hand of the third man was healed.
Once she was at Easter time. 'What shall we do?' said Brigit to her nuns.
'We have one measure of malt. It would be good for us to prepare it so that we would not be without ale at Easter.
There are also seventeen churches in Mag Tailach.
I wish that I could provide Easter for them with ale, for the sake of the Lord whose feast it is; even if they had no food, they would have drink.
Only it is unlucky for us that we have no vessels.' That was true: there was a single vessel in the house and two tubs.
'These are good; [?] enough.' This is what was done: they prepared the malt in one of the two tubs, and in the other tub it was poured off for straining;
and from what was poured off for straining into the tub the vessel was filled, and it was brought to each church in turn until the vessel came back again,
and as soon as it came back, what was in the tub was ale. Eighteen
vessels came from the one measure, and it supplied them at Easter;
and through that skill of Brigit there was no lack of a feast in any one of those churches from Great Easter to Little Easter.
On that day of Easter a faithful woman from Fid Éoin brought her a cow.
Two of them were driving the cow, the woman and her daughter. They were not able to drive their cow properly.
They let its calf loose as they came through the woodland. Then they prayed to Brigit [?].
That prayer did them some good: the cow itself led the way before them to the place where Brigit was.
"This is good, then," said Brigit to her girls,
"for this is our first offering since we took up this hermitage. Let it be taken to the bishop who blessed the veil on our heads."
"A cow without a calf is of little use to him," said the girls. "It will not be so," said Brigit.
"The little calf will come after its mother, so that they will reach the enclosure together." It was done just as she said.
On that same Sunday, Easter Sunday, a certain leper whose limbs were falling off came to her to ask for a cow.
"For the sake of God, Brigit, give me a cow." "Grant me a delay," said Brigit.
"I would not grant you even one day's delay," he said. "My little son," said Brigit, "let us wait for the hand of the Lord."
"I will go away," said the leper. "I will get a cow somewhere else, even if not from you."
"My dear [?]," said Brigit, "if we prayed to God to take your leprosy away from you, would you like that?"
"No," he said. "I get more in this state than I will when I am clean."
"It is better," said Brigit, "so take a blessing; you will be cleansed." "I am glad of it, then," he said,
"for what has taken hold of me is heavy." "How," said Brigit to her girls, "shall this man be cleansed?"
"It is not hard, nun: put your blessing on a cup of water, and then let the leper be bathed in it." It was done so, and he was completely healed.
"I will not go away, then," said the leper, "from the cup that healed me. I will be your servant and your woodcutter." And so it was.
On Monday, the next day, Mél came to Brigit to preach and to offer Mass between the two Easters.
A cow was given to her on that day as well. It too was given to Bishop Mél, after the other cow had been taken to him.
A fever came upon a girl of Brigit's community, so that it brought [?] upon her. "Is there anything you would like?" said Brigit.
"There is," she said. "Unless fresh milk comes to me, I will die now." Brigit called a girl to her and said:
"Bring me my own cup, the one I drink from, filled with water. Bring it hidden under your cloak."
It was brought to her, and she blessed it so that it became frothing [?] fresh milk, and the girl was completely healed at once when she tasted it.
So these are two miracles together: the making of milk from water, and the girl's healing.
On Tuesday, the next day, there was a good man nearby who was a kinsman of Brigit. He had been sick for a whole year.
"Take the best cow in the herd [?] to Brigit today," he said, "and let her pray to God for me so that I may be healed."
The cow was brought, and Brigit said to everyone who brought it: "Take it to Mél at once."
They brought her again to his house, and they bargained [?] over a cow while the sick man was away.
Brigit came to know of this. Brigit was angry [?] at the deceit over it. 'Between evening and morning,' said Brigit,
'wild dogs [?] will eat the good cow that was given into my possession and was not brought to you,' she said to Mel,
'and they will eat seven deer [?] along with it.' The sick man then came to know of this.
'Make amends, then,' he said; 'take seven deer [?] from the choicest of the herd [?].' That was done.
'Thanks be to God,' said Brigit. 'Let them be taken to Mel for his monastery. There are seven
days between the two Easters for preaching and saying Mass for us; so a cow each day for his work, and his gift is no greater than that;
and take a blessing with them, all nine [?], a blessing on everyone from whom they were given,' said Brigit.
When she had said this, he was healed at once.
Brigit found the stay between the two Easters hard to bear because of a headache. 'That will not last,' said Mel.
'When we go to visit our first foundation among the men of Tethba, Brigit will come with us, with her maidens.
There is a wonderful physician among the men of Meath, that is, Áed mac Bricc; he will cure you.'
It was there that she healed two paralysed virgins of the Fothairt.
Then two blind Britons came with a little leper boy of the race of Echu, and they earnestly asked for healing. Brigit said to them:
'Wait a little.' And they said: 'You have healed the sick of your own race, and you neglect to cure foreigners.'
'But at least heal our boy, who is of your race.' And because of this the blind were given sight and the leper was cleansed.
After that they reached Low Easter. 'I am not cheerful now,' said Brigit to her maidens,
'without ale on Low Easter for the bishop who has preached and who will say Mass.'
When she said this, two maidens went to the water to bring water into the house, taking a large vat with them for the preparation, and Brigit did not know.
When they came back, Brigit saw it there. 'Thanks be to God,' said Brigit.
'God has given us ale for our bishop.' At that the nuns were seized with fear.
'God help us, my daughters.' 'Whatever she has said, she has said nothing false or evil, nuns [?].'
'It was water that was brought into the house, but because you blessed it, God made [?] it,
and at once it was turned into ale with the scent of wine on it, and no better ale was ever poured into vessels in the world.'
Then the one vat was enough for the bishop and their guests.
Then, on the Monday after Little Easter, Brigit set out in her chariot. Her maidens went with her, along with the two bishops Mel and Melchu. They went into the Plain of Meath to see a physician,
and so that afterwards they might go on into the Plain of Tethba to revisit [?] a place that belonged to Mel and Melchu there.
And on Tuesday night they stopped at the house of a Leinsterman of the Uí Brolaig.
He took them in, looked kindly on them, and fed holy Brigit and the bishops.
That good man and his wife [?] were in distress. The wife said:
"Every child I have borne has died except two daughters, and they have been mute from the day they were born." She went to the Ford of Fergort.

Holy Brigit fell in the middle of the ford when the horses took fright, for what reason I do not know. Her holy head struck a stone and was wounded on the crown, and the blood that poured out freely reddened the water.
And holy Brigit said to one of the mute daughters: "Pour the water mixed with blood around your neck in the name of God."
She did so, and said: "You have healed me; I give thanks to God." "Call your sister," Brigit said to the girl who had been healed.
"Come with her, sister," she said. "I will come, then," said her sister. "I am healed, though I come [?].
I bowed down in the track of the chariot, and so I am healed." "Go [?] now," Brigit said to the girl,
"to your house. As many sons as have died in your family, you will bear the same number again."
There was rejoicing at that. And that famous stone often heals many people.
Anyone with a head sickness who lays their head on it is healed when they turn away from it.
Then they met the chief physician, Áed mac Bric. The bishop said:
"[Treat] the head of the holy maiden." He touched it and spoke to the virgin in these words:
"Virgin, the vein of your head has already been touched by a physician who is far better than I am."
They went to the men of Tethba, to the bishops' first foundation, that is, Ardagh.
The king of Tethba was holding a feast near them. A commoner in the king's house did a terrible thing.
The king's precious goblet fell from his hands and smashed against the table in front of the king.
The vessel was a marvellous one, one of the king's wonderful treasures. So the wretch was seized, and nothing awaited him but death.
One of the two bishops went to plead with the king. "I will not give him up to anyone," said the king,
"nor will I sell him either; there is nothing for him but death." "Let me have the broken vessel," said the bishop.
"You shall have that," said the king. Then the bishop carried it in his bosom to Brigit and told her everything.
"Pray to the Lord for us that the vessel may be made new." She did so, restored it, and gave it to the bishop;
And the next day the bishop came to the king with the vessel, and said: 'If your vessel has come back whole,' said the bishop,
'will you release the captive?' 'Not only that, but I would give him whatever gifts he wished.'
The bishop showed the vessel and spoke to the king like this: 'It was not I but Saint Brigit who worked this miracle.'
When Brigit's fame spread throughout Tethba, there was a certain devout virgin among the men of Tethba, Bríg daughter of Coimloch, who asked Brigit to come and talk with her.
So Brigit went, and Bríg came forward herself to wash her feet.
At that time there was a devout woman who was sick. While Bríg was washing Brigit's feet,
the sick woman who was in that house sent a girl to bring her some of the water from the basin that had been poured over Brigit's feet.
So it was brought to her, and she put it on her face and was immediately made completely well;
and although she had been sick for a year, that night she was one of those serving at table.
When their dishes were set before them, Brigit kept staring at the dishes.
'Tell us, holy girl,' said Bríg, 'what do you see on your dish?'
'I see Satan sitting on the dish in front of me,' said Brigit. 'If it is possible,' said Bríg,
'I would like to see him.' 'It is certainly possible,' said Brigit,
'but first make the sign of the cross over your eye, for anyone who sees the Devil without first signing themselves would be driven mad [?].'
So Bríg signed herself and saw that [?] creature. She found its shape hideous.
'Ask him, Brigit,' said Bríg, 'why he has come.' 'Give an answer to the people,' said Brigit.
'Not so, Brigit,' said Satan, 'it is not for you [?], for I have not come to harm you.'
'A question then,' said Bríg, 'what in particular brought you onto this dish?' The demon answered:
'I always live here with a certain virgin, whose great sloth has given me a place with her.'
And Bríg said: 'Let her be called.' When she had been called and came, Bríg said: 'Sign
her eyes, so that she may see the one she has nourished in her own bosom.' And when her eyes had been signed, she saw the horrible monster.
They were terrified, with fear and trembling. Brigit said: 'Look, you see the one you have cherished for many years and seasons.'
'Holy girl,' said Bríg, 'pray that he may not come into this house again.'
'He will not come into this house,' said Brigit, 'until Judgment Day.' They took their food and gave thanks to God.
Once she was [?] on the bank of the Inny. There were many apples and sweet sloes in that church.
There was another nun who brought a small gift [?] to her in a bark basket.
When she brought it into the house, lepers came at once onto the floor of the house to her, begging. 'Take,' she said,
'those apples.' Then the woman who had brought the fruit said: 'I did not give the gift to lepers.'
Brigit was displeased and said: 'You do wrong in withholding gifts from the servants of God; therefore your trees will bear no fruit for ever.'
And the giver, going outside, saw that her orchard at once bore not a single apple, though a little before it had been laden with fruit; and it remained barren for ever except for leaves.
There was another virgin who gave her apples and sweet sloes in abundance. She gave them at once to lepers who were begging.
'It will be health for the one who brought it [?],' said Brigit. 'Give then, O nun, a blessing on me and on my garden.' 'May God indeed bless,' said Brigit,
'the great tree yonder that I see in your garden; let there be sweet apples on it, and sweet sloes on a third of it;
and neither of those fruits will ever fail from it or from its offshoots.' And so it came about.
When the nun went into her garden she saw the alder tree with its fruit, and sweet sloes on a third of it.
In a certain place, namely Aicheth Fir Leth, two lepers followed Brigit. Contention seized them.
Quarrelling, they began to strike each other, but their hands and feet grew stiff. Seeing this, Brigit said:
'Do penance.' They did so. Not only did she release them, but she also healed them of leprosy.
It was then that two virgins came to Brigit so that she might go with them to consecrate their place and their house. Induae and Indiu were their names.
And on the road they met a young man who had come to speak with the nuns with whom Brigit was travelling. 'It is to you I have come,' he said,
'on behalf of this sick man, so that a chariot may be brought for him, so that it may be in the enclosure with you that death would come to him.'
'We have no chariot indeed,' said the nuns. 'Let my chariot be taken for him,' said Brigit.
That is what was done there. They were waiting until matins until the sick man came. Then lepers came to them in the morning.
'O Brigit,' they said, 'give us your chariot for Christ's sake.' 'Take it,' said Brigit.
'Grant us a delay, O servants of God, so that we may first bring the sick man to our house, which is near us.'
'We will not grant,' they said, 'even an hour's delay, unless [?] the chariot is taken from here at once.'
'Take it away,' said Brigit. 'What shall we do,' said the nuns, 'about the sick man?'
'Not difficult,' said Brigit. 'Let him come with us on his own feet.' That is what was done there. He was made completely whole at once.
It was then that she performed the washing of feet for the nuns of Cúl Fobair, so that she healed four
nuns at the foot-washing, namely: [?]; [?]; [?]; and a frenzied (mad) one.
It was then that she healed the lame, dumb boy at the house of Mac Odráin. It happened that only Brigit and the dumb boy were left there.
When some poor people came asking for a drink, holy Brigit looked for the key of the kitchen and could not find it.
Not knowing about the boy's illness, she said this: 'Where has the key been put?' And at that the dumb boy spoke, and the paralysed boy served them.
Shortly afterwards, as the beginning of summer came, Mel and Melchú said to Brigit: 'Look,
we have been told that Patrick has come from the south of Ireland into Mag Breg. Let us go and speak with him.
Will you go?' 'I will go,' said Brigit, 'so that I may see him and speak with him, and so that he may give me a blessing.'
When they set out on the road, a certain cleric with a great deal of goods and a household caught up with them on the road, to ask them for their company into Mag Breg.
'We are in a hurry,' said Mel, 'so that the cleric may not hold me back [?].' 'Let me find out from you,' said Brigit,
'the place where we will meet in Mag Breg, and I will stay with this wretched company.' So Brigit stayed with the travelling household.
'I have twenty girls with me on the road,' said Brigit. 'Give them some of the provisions [?].'
The poor people said: 'It shall not be so, for you have given us a greater gift, because thanks to you the road is safe for us.'
'Are there not two carts on the road?' said Brigit. 'Why are they not carrying the loads?'
For she had not looked to see what was in them. Since Brigit took up the religious life she did not look to either side, but only straight ahead of her.
'Indeed I have a brother,' said the cleric, 'in one of the carts, fourteen
years lame. I have a sister in the other one, blind.' 'That is sad,' said Brigit.
That night they came to a certain stream named Mana. Everyone ate of [?] except Brigit alone.
The next day she healed the two sick people who were travelling with them. The loads were put into the carts, and they gave thanks to God.
It was then that she healed the household of a commoner [?] on the seashore. So it was done.
There was another man working alone in a pasture [?]. The saint asked him why he was working alone. He said: 'My whole household is sick and in pain.'
When she heard this she blessed water, and at once healed the twelve sick people of his household.
Then they went to Tailtiu. Patrick was there.
They were dealing with a difficult question there: a certain woman had come to claim that a cleric of Patrick's community, named Bron, was the father of her son.
'How did this happen?' everyone asked. 'That is easy to tell,' said the woman.
'I came to Bron to have a veil blessed on my head and to offer my virginity to God.
This is what my cleric did: [?] me, so that I bore him a son.'
While they were at these words, it was then that she came to the assembly. It was then that Mel said to Patrick:
'The holy maiden, Brigit, is coming to the assembly;

you will know, through the greatness of her grace and the nearness of her miracles, whether this is true or false, for there is no deed between heaven and earth that she would ask of Christ,' said Mel,
'that would be refused to her. This is what is to be done for her there,' said Mel,
'to call her aside out of the assembly about this question, for she would not perform miracles in the presence of Saint Patrick.' Then Brigit came.
The crowd rose up before her. She was called aside out of the assembly at once to speak with the woman, and the clerics went with them, except Patrick.
'Whose is that child?' she said to the woman. 'Brón's,' said the woman. 'That is not true,' said Brigit.
Brigit made the sign of the cross over her face, so that her head swelled up on her, together with her tongue. At that moment Patrick came to them into the great assembly.
Brigit addressed the infant in front of the people of the assembly, although it had not yet begun to speak at that time.
'Who is your father?' said Brigit. The infant said:
'My father is not Bishop Brón, but a certain man who sits at the far end of the assembly, as the lowliest and ugliest; my mother is a liar.'
All gave thanks to God, and cried out that the wicked woman should be burned. But Brigit refused, saying: 'Let her do penance.'
This was done, and the swelling went down from her head and her tongue. The people rejoiced, the bishop was cleared, and Brigit was glorified.
When it was the end of the day, everyone went off in their own direction from the assembly to find lodging.
There was a good man on the bank of the river called the Suir. He sent his servant to the assembly to invite Brigit, saying to his household:
'The holy maiden who performed the wonderful miracle in the assembly today — I would like her to consecrate my house tonight.'
He welcomed her. 'Let it be brought, then,' said her maidens to Brigit,
'water for our hands; food is coming to us.' 'Not now,' said Brigit.
'For the Lord has shown me that this is a pagan household, except only the one servant who invited us. Because of that I will not eat now.'
The good man found this out, that is, that Brigit was fasting until he should be baptized.
'I have indeed said,' he said, 'that Patrick and his community would not baptize me.
But I will believe in you,' he said to Brigit. 'It is all the same to me, as long as you are baptized,' said Brigit.
'There is no man in holy orders with me,' said Brigit.
'Let someone go from us to Patrick, so that he may bring a bishop or a priest to baptize this man.'
Brón came and baptized the man together with his whole household at sunrise, and at midday they ate. They gave thanks.
They came to Saint Patrick. Patrick said: 'It is not lawful for you to travel without a priest.'
'Your charioteer must always be a priest.' And the abbots of Brigit kept this rule until recent times.
After that she healed the lame old woman who had been placed in the shelter of the chariot at Cell Suird in the south of Brega.
She healed the madman who had wandered through the territories. He was then brought to Brigit. When he saw her he was healed.
Then Brigit went to Cell Lassre. Lassair was glad to see her.
There was one milch sheep there, which had already been milked; it was slaughtered for Brigit.
At the end of the day they saw Patrick coming toward the enclosure. 'God help us, Brigit,' said Lassair.
'Give us advice.' Brigit answered: 'How much do you have?' She said:
'There is no food except twelve loaves, a little milk that you had blessed, and one little sheep that has been prepared for you.'
This is what happened: they all went to the meal, Patrick and Brigit, and everyone was satisfied;
and Lassair granted her church to her, and Brigit is venerated there.
She stayed the next day at Cell Lassre. A certain man of the Cennensis [?] kindred, whose wife had come to hate him, came to Brigit for help.
Brigit blessed water. He carried it with him, and once his wife had been sprinkled with it she immediately loved her husband passionately.
A certain pious virgin sent to Brigit asking Brigit to come and visit her.
Her name was Fine. Cell Fine was named after her. So Brigit went and stayed there.
One day while she was there, wind and rain and thunder and lightning broke out.
'Which of you girls will go out with your sheep today in this great storm?' All the girls alike refused.
Brigit answered: 'I love tending sheep very much.' 'I do not want you to go out,' said Fine. 'Let my will be done,' said Brigit.
Then she went out and recited a verse there: 'May I have a bright day from you, for you are dear, you are a king's son;
for at the vow of your mother Mary, forbid the rain, forbid the wind.
My King will do it for me: no rain will ever fall, because of Brigit, who goes out here today to the herding.' She calmed the rain and the wind. The end.

The king of Leinster gave a brooch to a poet as a pledge, and the poet gave it into the keeping of his slave-woman. Then he stole it out of malice toward the slave-woman, because [?] he desired her [?].
Then someone came from the king to redeem his brooch. The druid went to kill the slave-woman because he did not find the brooch.
Then Brigit came to the house, and she was grieved by this. She prayed, and the angel revealed to her what had happened to the brooch. Brigit said:
'Put the nets into the water, and a salmon will be found in them with the brooch inside it.'
And so it was done, and afterwards the maidservant was freed through the grace of Saint Brigit.
Three brothers were given an ingot of silver by their father, and the smiths of Leinster could not divide it.
Brigit divided it so that no share was more or less than another. She worked that miracle at Kildare.
Three strong men were building the rampart of Aillenn: Muiredach, Fiacha and Lugaid.
Each of them would eat a meal meant for a hundred. Lugaid was working on behalf of the churches; the other two on behalf of the laity.
Lugaid came to Brigit, and she cooked a lamb for him and blessed his mouth, so that he needed no more to fill him than any other man,
and he lifted into the rampart the stone that every man had failed to lift the day before. That is why it is called Aillenn, that is, ail find, 'white stone'.
A man of her community owed ale to the king of Leinster.
The man came to Brigit lamenting and asked her to help him, because he had nothing to pay it with.
Then he put water into the vat beside Brigit's house, and Brigit blessed the water, and afterwards it was mead,
and the poor man brought it to the king, and there was no sweeter mead. There was neither more nor less of it than was owed.
Conlaed, Brigit's craftsman, set out for Rome.
This was the reason: while he was away, Brigit had given his cowl to a leper. At that time he was forging the bell and Brigit was minding his workshop.
Conlaed asked Brigit for his garment, and Brigit asked Ronchenn —
that is, a subdeacon who always kept her clothing — whether he had a garment.
'Let her say a prayer,' he said, 'and there will be one.' Then she said a prayer, and a garment was found in Ronchenn's chest.
Afterwards Conlaed set off to go to Rome. She said to him: 'You will not get there, and you will not come back here.'
And so it was done: wild dogs devoured him at Sciath Chomgaill, or Sciath Chonlaid, in the east of Mag Life.
Brendan of the sea spent seven years on the open sea.
During that time two sea-monsters kept company with his boat. One of them was attacking, and the other was holding it back.
One of them called on Patrick and the other elders of Ireland to protect it against its enemy.
It called on Brendan as well, but it got nothing from him. Last of all it called on Brigit. Then the stronger monster was silenced.
'Listen to this, clerics,' said Brendan when he told the story afterwards.
They return to Ireland. They go ashore. 'Come with us to Brigit,' said Brendan.
At that time Brigit was on the Curragh of the Liffey, south of Kildare.
Brendan comes to a meeting [?] at Domnach Mór, west of Kildare, after the angel had instructed him. He is welcomed at Lig Brenaind (Brendan's Bed).
After that they went to Kildare. Brigit throws her wet cowl over the sunbeams.
Brendan's servant puts the cloak that Brendan was wearing over them, and it fell off them.
He puts it on again, and they did not hold it. Brendan himself rose and arranged it on them, and it stayed like that.
Brendan asked Brigit what labour she did for her Lord. 'Tell me first,' said Brigit,
'the male has the right to go first.' 'By our confession,' said Brendan, 'I have never crossed seven
furrows without my mind being on God.' 'Thanks be to God,' said Brigit.
'The Son of the Virgin knows that since I gave my mind to him I have not taken it away from him until now.'
'It is no wonder,' said Brendan, 'if the sea-beasts praised above everyone the one who is in that service.'
Her cook [?] comes to the nun. 'Do you have any [food]?' she said. 'There is none,' he said, 'except an eighth-measure [?] of barley grain.'
'Thanks be to God,' said Brigit. 'Take it to be ground at the mill of Ráith Cathair, west of Kildare.'
The millers refused to grind his bag. He goes to Brigit.
'Go now,' she said. He goes, and his journey was not successful.
He returns to Brigit. 'Go again,' she said. He turns back.
The miller took his bag off his back and threw it into the mill-pond. He went weeping to Brigit.
She cursed the millwright and the mill, and asked God to destroy them both; and so it was done.
The young man comes with his meal-bag on his back. The meal was half and half, that is, meal for food and meal for ale.
Ailill son of Dúnlaing was in Kildare when these miracles were done. They spent thirty days consuming it, both women and men. The end.
